concepts.name: Definition and Debate on Deindustrialisation
key_dimensions: R.C. Dutt vs. modern historians on whether deindustrialisation was absolute or relative
Distinction between deindustrialisation as decline in absolute numbers vs. share of workforce
Tirthankar Roy's revisionist argument: some handicrafts survived and adapted — UPSC trap on 'total collapse' framing
Amiya Bagchi's statistical evidence using occupational data from Gangetic Bihar as empirical proof

concepts.name: One-Way Free Trade Policy and Asymmetric Tariff Structure
key_dimensions: British manufactured goods entered India at low or zero tariffs while Indian exports faced protective tariffs in Britain
Abolition of Company's trade monopoly in 1813 and opening of India to British manufacturers
Counterfactual: how protective tariffs could have preserved Indian industries (comparison with Meiji Japan)
UPSC trap: distinguishing between free trade ideology and its selective/asymmetric application by Britain

concepts.name: Manchester Textile Industry vs. Indian Handloom — The Central Case Study
key_dimensions: How machine-made British cloth undercut Indian handloom on price despite quality differences
Role of power loom and Industrial Revolution in creating structural cost advantage for British textiles
Dacca Muslin as the iconic example of a luxury craft destroyed — causes, timeline, and exaggeration debate
Survival pockets: Banarasi silk, Kanjeevaram, Pochampalli — why some survived and others did not

concepts.name: Dacca Muslin: Myth, Reality, and Historiographical Controversy
key_dimensions: The 'thumbs of weavers cut off' narrative — historical evidence vs. nationalist myth-making
Actual causes of decline: loss of Mughal court patronage, cheaper British substitutes, loss of skilled artisan base
Significance as a symbol in nationalist economic critique (Dadabhai Naoroji, R.C. Dutt)
UPSC trap: questions that ask for 'main cause' — patronage loss vs. British competition vs. raw material diversion

concepts.name: Drain of Wealth Theory and Its Link to Deindustrialisation
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901) — mechanism of drain
How Home Charges and repatriation of profits denied reinvestment capital to Indian industries
Distinction between drain theory and deindustrialisation — overlapping but separate phenomena
R.C. Dutt's 'Economic History of India' as the bridge connecting trade policy, drain, and industrial decline

concepts.name: Railway Expansion: Dual Role as Facilitator and Destroyer
key_dimensions: Railways as a channel for British manufactured goods to penetrate deep into Indian hinterlands
Simultaneous destruction of local cart-making, iron-smelting, and regional craft clusters
Paradox: railways also enabled Indian raw materials to reach ports faster, boosting British mills
UPSC trap: Railways as both a modernising force AND an instrument of deindustrialisation — avoid one-sided answers

concepts.name: Colonial Land Revenue Policy and Its Impact on Artisan Classes
key_dimensions: Permanent Settlement (1793) and Ryotwari systems forcing artisans into agriculture due to economic distress
High land revenue demands reducing purchasing power of rural population — shrinking domestic market for handicrafts
Conversion of artisans from craft producers to agricultural labourers or distressed cultivators
Link between agrarian crises (famines) and accelerated craft abandonment

concepts.name: Loss of Princely and Mughal Court Patronage
key_dimensions: Mughal imperial decline post-Aurangzeb removing the apex demand node for luxury crafts
Doctrine of Lapse and annexation of princely states eliminating regional court patronage systems
Shift of elite consumption preference to European goods as a status symbol — demand-side deindustrialisation
UPSC angle: distinguishing political causes (patronage loss) from economic causes (tariff/trade) of craft decline

concepts.name: Raw Material Export and Input Deprivation for Indian Craftsmen
key_dimensions: Export of raw cotton, silk, and indigo to Britain depriving Indian weavers of affordable inputs
Price inflation of raw materials at home due to export demand — cost-push squeeze on artisans
Indigo cultivation forced on peasants diverting agricultural land — indirect impact on craft input chains
Comparison: Indian iron ore exported while Indian iron-smelting industry simultaneously declined

concepts.name: Selective Survival and Adaptation of Handicrafts — The Revisionist View
key_dimensions: Tirthankar Roy's argument: handicrafts that served niche, religious, or export markets survived
Silk weaving, brassware, pottery — cases of adaptation to colonial economy rather than pure decline
Role of Arts and Crafts movement and colonial exhibitions (1851 Crystal Palace) in creating new export demand
UPSC trap: 'deindustrialisation was complete and total' is an oversimplification — nuanced answer required

concepts.name: Iron and Steel Craft Decline — Pre-Industrial Indian Metallurgy
key_dimensions: Wootz steel (Damascus steel) and its global reputation before colonial period
How cheap British iron imports destroyed indigenous smelting and forging industries
Absence of colonial investment in modernising Indian metallurgy vs. deliberate neglect argument
Contrast with post-independence Tata Steel — irony of India rebuilding what colonialism destroyed

concepts.name: Occupational Census Data and Statistical Evidence of Deindustrialisation
key_dimensions: Amiya Bagchi's use of 1809–13 Francis Buchanan surveys vs. 1901 Census data for Gangetic Bihar
Limitations of colonial census data in capturing informal craft employment — methodological debate
Decline in percentage of population engaged in secondary sector as proxy for deindustrialisation
UPSC angle: 'Which economist provided statistical evidence?' type factual traps

concepts.name: Gender Dimension of Deindustrialisation
key_dimensions: Women's role in spinning (charkha) decimated by machine-spun yarn imports — gendered economic displacement
Gandhi's symbolic revival of spinning as both economic programme and political resistance
Differential impact on female artisans vs. male artisans across different craft sectors
Link between loss of women's supplementary income and increased rural household poverty

concepts.name: The Swadeshi Movement as a Response to Deindustrialisation
key_dimensions: 1905 Swadeshi Movement explicitly invoking craft revival and boycott of British goods as connected goals
Distinction between Swadeshi as economic programme vs. political movement — UPSC often conflates
Role of intellectuals like Rabindranath Tagore and Bal Gangadhar Tilak in framing craft revival ideologically
Limited economic success but significant consciousness-raising — 'means vs. ends' analytical question

concepts.name: Nationalist Economic Critique: Naoroji, Dutt, and Ranade
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji: 'poverty' rooted in drain — first systematic critique linking trade to de-industrialisation
R.C. Dutt: focus on land revenue and trade policy as twin destroyers of Indian crafts and agriculture
M.G. Ranade: advocated industrialisation and state support — contrast with Gandhi's village industry approach
UPSC trap: attributing specific arguments to wrong economists — Naoroji ≠ Dutt ≠ Ranade on solutions

concepts.name: Absence of Protective Tariffs and the Indian Industrial Commission (1916–18)
key_dimensions: Indian Industrial Commission appointed during WWI acknowledging Britain's deliberate neglect of Indian industry
Fiscal Autonomy Convention (1919) — India gaining limited right to impose tariffs, and its significance
Post-WWI tariff protection for Indian cotton mills as a belated and partial reversal
UPSC trap: Fiscal Autonomy Convention date, context, and whether it reversed deindustrialisation — it did not fully

concepts.name: Comparative Deindustrialisation: India vs. Other Colonial Economies
key_dimensions: Comparison with Egypt's cotton industry — similar pattern of raw material export, craft decline
Contrast with Japan: Meiji industrialisation with protective tariffs showing the 'road not taken' for India
Mike Davis ('Late Victorian Holocausts') framing deindustrialisation within global capitalist expansion
UPSC angle: 'Was deindustrialisation unique to India?' — answer requires comparative global perspective

concepts.name: Impact of Deindustrialisation on Urbanisation and Town Decline
key_dimensions: Decline of craft-based towns: Murshidabad, Surat, Dhaka lost population as industries collapsed
Rise of new colonial port cities (Bombay, Calcutta, Madras) vs. decline of traditional manufacturing towns
Reverse urbanisation or 'ruralisation' — artisans forced back to villages and agriculture
UPSC angle: connecting deindustrialisation to the broader colonial restructuring of Indian spatial economy

concepts.name: Gandhi's Constructive Programme and Khadi as Counter-Narrative
key_dimensions: Charkha and Khadi as direct political-economic response to machine-textile deindustrialisation
Gandhi's critique of industrial civilisation vs. Nehru-Ambedkar's pro-industrialisation counter-argument
Economic viability of Khadi programme — symbolic power vs. structural economic solution debate
UPSC trap: Gandhi's position on deindustrialisation blamed industrialism broadly, NOT just British industry — nuance matters

concepts.name: Legacy of Deindustrialisation: Impact on Post-Independence Economic Planning
key_dimensions: Nehruvian heavy industrialisation strategy as a direct response to colonial deindustrialisation experience
Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) — institutional legacy of Gandhian craft revival
Debate in Constituent Assembly and Planning Commission on small-scale vs. large-scale industry
UPSC angle: How colonial deindustrialisation shaped Article 43 (DPSP on cottage industries) and Five-Year Plan priorities
